issues.legal_issue: An authenticated government sanction order may be proved as a public document, and its admissibility cannot ordinarily be challenged for the first time on appeal after it was admitted without objection at trial.
material_facts: The prosecution produced the original government order authorizing prosecution, issued in the name of the Governor and authenticated by a government secretary.
The order stated that the competent authority had examined the material and considered prosecution appropriate.
A witness identified the secretary’s signature, and cross-examination did not undermine his ability to identify it.
The order’s authenticity was not disputed, and the defence did not object to its admission at trial.
issues.conclusion: The sanction order was admissible and sufficiently proved; the High Court erred in holding that it had not been proved in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 19 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, prosecution requires sanction from the competent authority. An authenticated executive order issued in the Governor’s name is a public document under Section 74 of the Indian Evidence Act and may be proved under Sections 76 to 78; proof is not confined to the opinion evidence contemplated by Section 47. Under Section 67, handwriting may be proved by any lawful mode. Gulzar Ali v. State of H.P. explains that handwriting may be established by modes other than Sections 45 and 47. A valid sanction may be proved by producing the original order containing the offence facts and grounds for satisfaction, or by other evidence showing that those facts were placed before the authority and satisfaction was reached, as held in Mohd. Iqbal Ahmed v. State of Andhra Pradesh. R.J. Singh Ahuluwalia v. State of Delhi concerned the absence of sanction by the competent authority. An objection to admissibility not raised when the document was admitted cannot be raised for the first time on appeal, as supported by Ranvir Singh v. Union of India.

rule.if: corruption_prosecution and (authenticated_original_sanction_order and competent_authority_considered_material and signature_identified and order_authenticity_unchallenged and no_trial_objection)

predicates.corruption_prosecution: The prosecution was brought for alleged corruption offences for which prior government approval was required.
predicates.authenticated_original_sanction_order: The prosecution produced an original government approval order authenticated as an official executive act.
predicates.competent_authority_considered_material: The order recorded that the authority empowered to remove the accused had examined the material and considered prosecution appropriate.
predicates.signature_identified: A witness identified the signature of the official who authenticated the order, and cross-examination did not undermine that identification.
predicates.order_authenticity_unchallenged: The opposing party did not dispute the authenticity of the official order.
predicates.no_trial_objection: The opposing party allowed the order to be admitted at trial without objection and challenged its admissibility only on appeal.

issues.definition: When a corruption prosecution relies on an authenticated original approval order that reflects the competent authority’s consideration, whose signature is identified and whose authenticity and admission were not challenged at trial, the order is admissible and proven.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal in a prosecution appeal should stand when the evidence permits two views and the view supporting acquittal is not wholly improbable.
material_facts: The complainant alleged that the accused demanded money, but the application and supporting records were processed rapidly and the accused sent the valuation certificate onward despite the alleged demand remaining unpaid.
The accused was only a recommending official; another official evaluated the property and a superior official granted the certificate.
The complainant had direct access to the superior official and had obtained records and certifications quickly, yet did not promptly complain about the alleged demand.
The timing and circumstances of the complaint and trap, and the handling of additional cash found in the accused’s pocket, raised doubts about the prosecution account.
The High Court found the prosecution case unproved and acquitted the accused; the Supreme Court concluded that two views were possible and the acquittal view was not wholly improbable.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court sustained the acquittal and dismissed the State’s appeal because the evidence did not compel the conclusion that the accused was guilty.
issues.legal_principle: Where the evidence in an appeal from acquittal permits two possible views and the view taken by the acquitting court is not wholly improbable, the acquittal should not be disturbed. The Court applied that approach to the doubts in the prosecution evidence and the circumstances surrounding the alleged demand and trap; it cited no earlier case for this determination.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and prosecution_evidence_has_material_doubts and (two_views_possible and acquittal_view_not_wholly_improbable)

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution appealed against a judgment acquitting the accused.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_has_material_doubts: The evidence about the alleged demand and trap contained circumstances that cast doubt on the prosecution account.
predicates.two_views_possible: The evidence reasonably supported both a guilty view and a view consistent with acquittal.
predicates.acquittal_view_not_wholly_improbable: The factual view adopted by the court that acquitted the accused was not wholly improbable.

issues.definition: When a prosecution appeal challenges an acquittal, material doubts leave two views possible, and the acquittal view is not wholly improbable, the acquittal is upheld.
